title: Victim in Brampton police shooting is Jermaine Carby, says mother
subtitle: The man was pulled over by a Peel police officer near Queen St. E. and Kennedy Rd. around 10 p.m.
article: At 6 p.m. on Wednesday, Lorna Robinson was with her son, Jermaine Carby, eating chips and dip, chatting about the day, and even doing a little bit of exercise.
At 3 a.m., an investigator with the Special Investigations Unit woke her up with a knock at the door. She says she hasn't slept since.
Robinson said the investigator told her that her son, the eldest of two, was the victim in Wednesday night's shooting involving police in Brampton.
While mourning the loss of her son, Robinson also finds herself on the defensive, saying people should not believe reports from British Columbia that her son was an infamous drug enforcer.
"I don't know exactly what was going on," she said of Wednesday's shooting. "I want to see justice served. I want to see justice done."

Peel police previously confirmed that an officer pulled over a vehicle at the Queen St. E. and Kennedy Rd. intersection around 10 p.m. Following an interaction with police, an occupant in the vehicle was shot on the street.

Within minutes of shots being fired, a total of 30 police cars were on scene. The victim died in hospital. A witness at the scene told the Star he saw police take the driver of the vehicle away in handcuffs.

The SIU, an arm's-length agency that investigates police-related incidents involving death, serious injury and allegations of sexual assault, says it is not publicly releasing the name of the victim out of respect for his family. Peel police is not commenting on the case because the SIU has invoked its mandate.

After spending several hours with her son on Wednesday, Robinson said she returned home and Carby told her he was going out with a friend, who she believes was in the car with Carby, 33, when it was pulled over by police. She said reports circulating her son was carrying a knife at the time of his interaction with police are false.
"As far as I'm concerned, my son was a gentle person, a loving person, a family person," she said.

Born in Toronto, Carby attended Catholic schools, according to Robinson, adding he was very intelligent and loved to read. She said when Carby was about 20, he left Toronto to start over in B.C., saying he wanted to go to law school. His mother said she believes he was enrolled at the University of British Columbia.

Carby's name was widely circulated in late 2011 when Vancouver police announced they had arrested a man by that name for assault on two women in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside and for manslaughter in the stabbing death of a 50-year-old man.

At the time, Vancouver Police Insp. Brad Desmarais told the Vancouver Sun that Carby was "one of the most well-known street-level enforcers in the Downtown Eastside, with a long history of violence, drug trafficking and drug possession." Vancouver police said in 2011 Carby had had 110 interactions with police, with a criminal record dating back to 2000 in Toronto.
When asked about the police accounts, Robinson said "none of it is true."

"They tried to frame him," she said, adding Carby didn't speak to her for some time while he was living in B.C. because "he didn't want to get me involved. He was the type of person who didn't want to hurt anyone's feelings." She did, however, travel to that province several years ago on her 50th birthday to visit him.

On Thursday, Vancouver police spokesman Const. Brian Montague said he could not confirm that the man shot in Brampton is the same Jermaine Carby arrested in Vancouver in 2011, but said "a person by that name and the same age is the person we dealt with on Sept. 9, 2011, for the stabbing death of a 50-year-old man in the park."

There is no indication in British Columbia's online court registry that a verdict was rendered on the assault and manslaughter charges. A provincial Ministry of Justice spokesman said he was "unable to confirm whether an individual is or was in our custody or under our supervision," due to privacy concerns. Court documents do show that Carby was found guilty of uttering threats in 2012 and possession for the purpose of trafficking in 2008 and 2009.

Robinson said her son came back to the GTA from B.C. in October 2012 to help her out. She said Carby's father died several years ago of a heart attack. Robinson, who is struggling to pay for her son's funeral, said Carby had recently been trying to turn his life around, hoping to go back to school soon and become an electrician.
"He was always close to my heart, and was always my company," she said. "Now I'm left with one (son). Inside of me is empty."
